questiontext.text: What does pairwise (2-way) testing require of a test suite?

answer.text: For every pair of parameters, every combination of their values appears together in at least one test

feedback.text: Correct — that is exactly the 2-way coverage guarantee.

answer.text: Every possible combination of all parameter values appears in some test

feedback.text: That is exhaustive testing; pairwise only covers value pairs, not full combinations.

answer.text: Each individual parameter value appears in at least one test

feedback.text: That is weaker (each-choice) coverage; pairwise additionally requires every pair of values.

answer.text: Exactly two tests are run for each parameter

feedback.text: Pairwise constrains which value pairs are covered, not a fixed number of tests per parameter.

generalfeedback.text: Pairwise (2-way) testing requires that for every pair of parameters, every combination of one value from each appears together in at least one test case. It targets two-way interaction faults while using far fewer tests than exhaustive coverage.

questiontext.text: What empirical observation motivates pairwise testing?

answer.text: Most software faults are triggered by a single factor or by an interaction of only two factors

feedback.text: Correct — studies of the interaction/fault-coupling of defects show most failures involve one or two factors.

answer.text: Most software faults require every parameter to take an extreme value simultaneously

feedback.text: On the contrary, high-order interactions cause relatively few faults; that is why pairwise pays off.

answer.text: Faults are distributed uniformly across all combinations of parameters

feedback.text: If faults were uniform across full combinations, pairwise would offer little benefit; the evidence is that low-order interactions dominate.

answer.text: Faults only ever depend on a single input parameter

feedback.text: Two-way (and occasionally higher) interactions do occur; pairwise targets the common one- and two-factor cases.

generalfeedback.text: Empirical fault studies found that a large majority of failures are caused by a single factor or a two-factor interaction, with progressively fewer caused by three or more factors. Pairwise testing exploits this by guaranteeing all two-way combinations at low cost.

questiontext.text: For a system configured by several parameters, what does exhaustive combinatorial testing require?

answer.text: One test for every possible combination of values across all parameters

feedback.text: Correct — exhaustive means the full Cartesian product of the parameter domains.

answer.text: One test for every pair of parameter values

feedback.text: That is pairwise testing, a small subset of exhaustive.

answer.text: One test per parameter

feedback.text: That does not even cover each value; exhaustive covers every full combination.

answer.text: A fixed number of tests regardless of the number of parameters

feedback.text: Exhaustive count grows as the product of the domain sizes, so it depends heavily on the parameters.

generalfeedback.text: Exhaustive testing runs every combination of parameter values — the full Cartesian product. Its size is the product of all the domain sizes, which grows explosively, which is the very problem combinatorial testing addresses.

questiontext.text: A feature has three parameters: the first has 3 possible values, the second has 2, and the third has 2. How many tests does exhaustive testing require?

feedback.text: Correct — 3 × 2 × 2 = 12, the product of the domain sizes.
7 is the sum 3 + 2 + 2; exhaustive multiplies the domain sizes.
6 counts only two of the three parameters (3 × 2); include the third.
4 is the product of the two largest domains (3 × 2 would be 6, not 4), and in any case that is a pairwise lower bound, not the exhaustive count.

generalfeedback.text: Exhaustive testing is the product of all domain sizes: 3 × 2 × 2 = 12.

questiontext.text: A configuration has three parameters, each with 3 possible values. How many tests does exhaustive testing require?

feedback.text: Correct — 3 × 3 × 3 = 27.
9 is 3 × 3, the product of only two parameters (and it is the pairwise lower bound here), not the full product.
6 is 3 + 3 (two parameters summed); exhaustive multiplies all three domain sizes.
81 is 3 to the fourth power, i.e. four parameters; here there are only three.

generalfeedback.text: Exhaustive count is the product of all domain sizes: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27.

questiontext.text: A function has two parameters: one with 4 possible values and one with 3. How many tests does exhaustive testing require?

feedback.text: Correct — 4 × 3 = 12.
7 is the sum 4 + 3; exhaustive multiplies the domain sizes.
16 is 4 × 4; the second parameter has 3 values, not 4.
9 is 3 × 3; the first parameter has 4 values, not 3.

generalfeedback.text: With two parameters the exhaustive count equals the product of the two domain sizes: 4 × 3 = 12. (With only two parameters, exhaustive and pairwise coincide.)

questiontext.text: Pairwise testing is the case t = 2 of t-way (combinatorial) testing. What does general t-way testing require?

answer.text: Every combination of values among every group of t parameters appears in at least one test

feedback.text: Correct — strength t means all t-tuples of values are covered.

answer.text: Every parameter takes exactly t different values across the suite

feedback.text: t is the interaction strength, not the number of values a parameter takes.

answer.text: The suite contains exactly t test cases

feedback.text: t is the strength of coverage, not the number of tests.

answer.text: At most t parameters are tested at a time and the rest are ignored

feedback.text: All parameters are covered; t is the size of the interacting groups whose combinations must all appear.

generalfeedback.text: t-way testing generalizes pairwise: for strength t, every combination of values across every set of t parameters must appear in at least one test. t = 1 is each-choice, t = 2 is pairwise, and t equal to the number of parameters is exhaustive.

questiontext.text: In combinatorial testing, what is a covering array?

answer.text: A set of test rows in which every t-way combination of parameter values appears in at least one row

feedback.text: Correct — a covering array of strength t guarantees every t-tuple appears at least once.

answer.text: A table listing every possible combination of parameter values exactly once

feedback.text: That is the exhaustive set; a covering array is usually much smaller and only requires each t-tuple at least once.

answer.text: An array recording which test found which fault

feedback.text: That is a fault matrix, not a covering array.

answer.text: A matrix of code-coverage percentages for each test

feedback.text: Covering arrays describe input-value combinations, not structural code coverage.

generalfeedback.text: A covering array is a compact set of test rows over the parameters such that every combination of values for every group of t parameters appears in at least one row. For pairwise, t = 2.

name.text: Meaning of t in CA(N; t, k, v)

questiontext.text: In the covering-array notation CA(N; t, k, v), what does the parameter t denote?

answer.text: The interaction strength — the size of the parameter groups whose value combinations must all be covered

feedback.text: Correct — t is the strength; t = 2 is pairwise.

answer.text: The number of test rows in the array

feedback.text: That is N, the number of rows.

answer.text: The number of parameters (factors)

feedback.text: That is k, the number of factors.

answer.text: The number of values each parameter can take

feedback.text: That is v, the number of levels per factor.

generalfeedback.text: In CA(N; t, k, v): N is the number of rows, t is the interaction strength, k is the number of parameters (factors), and v is the number of values (levels) each takes. Pairwise corresponds to t = 2.

questiontext.text: "Pairwise testing" and "2-way combinatorial testing" refer to the same thing.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — pairwise is exactly t-way testing with t = 2.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: They are the same: pairwise is the special case t = 2 of t-way combinatorial testing.

generalfeedback.text: Pairwise testing is 2-way combinatorial testing: it guarantees that every pair of values across every pair of parameters is covered at least once.

questiontext.text: Exhaustive combinatorial testing covers every possible combination of all parameter values, and its test count is the product of all the domain sizes.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — exhaustive is the full Cartesian product, sized as the product of the domains.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Exhaustive testing does run every combination, and that count is exactly the product of the domain sizes.

generalfeedback.text: Exhaustive testing runs the full Cartesian product of the parameter domains; its size is the product of all domain sizes, which is why it becomes infeasible as parameters grow.

questiontext.text: In pairwise testing, what exactly is the "pair" that must be covered?

answer.text: A specific value of one parameter together with a specific value of another parameter

feedback.text: Correct — a pair is one value from each of two parameters, covered together in a test.

answer.text: Two test cases that must be run consecutively

feedback.text: A pair refers to a combination of parameter values, not to two test cases.

answer.text: Two different values of the same parameter

feedback.text: A pair spans two different parameters, one value from each.

answer.text: A valid input paired with its expected output

feedback.text: That describes a test oracle, not the pair covered by pairwise testing.

generalfeedback.text: A pair is one value of one parameter combined with one value of a second parameter. Pairwise coverage requires every such pair, over every choice of two parameters, to appear together in at least one test.

questiontext.text: Why is exhaustive combinatorial testing usually impractical for real systems?

answer.text: The number of combinations is the product of the domain sizes, which grows explosively as parameters are added

feedback.text: Correct — combinatorial explosion makes the full product infeasible.

answer.text: Exhaustive testing cannot detect any interaction faults

feedback.text: Exhaustive testing actually detects all interaction faults; the problem is its cost, not its power.

answer.text: Each combination must be tested thousands of times to be valid

feedback.text: Each combination is tested once; the issue is the sheer number of combinations.

answer.text: Test tools cannot represent more than two parameters at once

feedback.text: Tools handle many parameters; the obstacle is the exponential number of combinations.

generalfeedback.text: Exhaustive testing multiplies all the domain sizes, so the count explodes as parameters and values grow (for example ten binary parameters already require 2^10 = 1024 tests). Pairwise testing keeps the guarantee for two-way interactions while cutting the count dramatically.

questiontext.text: What interaction strength t characterizes pairwise testing?

feedback.text: Correct — pairwise means all two-parameter value combinations are covered.
t = 1 is each-choice coverage (every single value), weaker than pairwise.
t = 3 is three-way testing, stronger and more costly than pairwise.

answer.text: t equals the number of parameters

feedback.text: t equal to the number of parameters is exhaustive testing, not pairwise.

generalfeedback.text: Pairwise testing has strength t = 2: it guarantees coverage of all value combinations among every group of two parameters.

questiontext.text: A valid pairwise test suite must include every pair of parameter values at least once, but it need not include each pair more than once.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — the requirement is "at least once"; repetition is allowed but not required.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Pairwise coverage requires each pair at least once; covering some pairs more than once is permitted but not necessary.

generalfeedback.text: Pairwise (covering-array) coverage requires each value pair to appear at least once. Requiring each pair the same fixed number of times would be an orthogonal array — a stronger, balanced special case.

name.text: Exhaustive count for 4 x 3 x 3 x 2

questiontext.text: A system has four parameters with domain sizes 4, 3, 3, and 2. How many tests does exhaustive testing require?

feedback.text: 12 is the product of only the two largest domains (4 × 3), which is the pairwise lower bound, not the exhaustive count.
36 is 4 × 3 × 3; it omits the last parameter (× 2).

answer.text: 12 + others

feedback.text: Exhaustive is a product, not a sum: 4 × 3 × 3 × 2 = 72.

generalfeedback.text: Exhaustive testing is the product of all domain sizes: 4 × 3 × 3 × 2 = 72.

name.text: Pairwise lower bound for 3 x 3 x 2

questiontext.text: A configuration has three parameters with domain sizes 3, 3, and 2. What is the minimum number of tests any pairwise (2-way) suite must contain?

answer.text: At least 9

feedback.text: Correct — the lower bound is the product of the two largest domains, 3 × 3 = 9.

answer.text: At least 18

feedback.text: 18 is the exhaustive count (3 × 3 × 2); pairwise needs far fewer.

answer.text: At least 3

feedback.text: 3 (the largest single domain) only satisfies each-choice coverage, not all pairs.

answer.text: At least 6

feedback.text: 6 is below the bound: covering all 3 × 3 = 9 pairs of the two 3-valued parameters already forces at least 9 rows.

generalfeedback.text: To cover every pair from the two 3-valued parameters you already need all 3 × 3 = 9 of their combinations, so any pairwise suite has at least 9 rows. The lower bound is the product of the two largest domains.

name.text: Why the two largest domains give the bound

questiontext.text: Why is the minimum size of any pairwise suite at least the product of the two largest parameter domains?

answer.text: Every pair from those two parameters must appear, and there are (largest × second-largest) such pairs, each needing its own row

feedback.text: Correct — no single row can cover two distinct value-pairs of the same two parameters, so you need at least that many rows.

answer.text: Because the smallest domains determine how many rows are reusable

feedback.text: The bound comes from the largest domains, since they generate the most pairs to cover.

answer.text: Because each parameter needs one row per value regardless of the others

feedback.text: That reasoning gives each-choice, not the pairwise bound from the two largest domains.

answer.text: Because the suite must equal the exhaustive product divided by two

feedback.text: There is no such division rule; the bound is the product of the two largest domains.

generalfeedback.text: Consider just the two parameters with the largest domains. Their pairs number (largest × second-largest), and a single test row fixes one value for each, so it covers only one of those pairs. Hence at least (largest × second-largest) rows are required — that product is the pairwise lower bound.

questiontext.text: How does the AETG algorithm construct a pairwise test suite?

answer.text: Greedily, adding one whole test row at a time that covers as many still-uncovered pairs as possible

feedback.text: Correct — AETG is a greedy one-row-at-a-time heuristic.

answer.text: By enumerating every combination and then deleting redundant rows

feedback.text: AETG never enumerates the full product; it builds rows greedily to avoid that explosion.

answer.text: By solving an exact integer program that guarantees the minimum suite

feedback.text: AETG is a heuristic; it is near-optimal, not guaranteed minimal.

answer.text: By adding one parameter column at a time to a growing array

feedback.text: That describes IPOG's one-parameter-at-a-time strategy, not AETG.

generalfeedback.text: AETG (Automatic Efficient Test Generator) greedily builds the suite one complete test row at a time, each time choosing a row that covers as many yet-uncovered pairs as possible. It is fast and near-optimal but not guaranteed to produce the smallest possible suite.

questiontext.text: What is the defining strategy of the IPOG algorithm?

answer.text: In-Parameter-Order growth: build the array for the first parameters, then extend it one parameter at a time, filling and adding rows to cover new pairs

feedback.text: Correct — IPOG grows the array horizontally (add a parameter) then vertically (add rows) as needed.

answer.text: It randomly samples rows until all pairs happen to be covered

feedback.text: IPOG is deterministic and constructive, not random sampling.

answer.text: It computes the exact minimal covering array by exhaustive search

feedback.text: IPOG is a greedy heuristic; it is near-optimal, not guaranteed minimal.

answer.text: It tests one parameter in isolation and ignores interactions

feedback.text: IPOG explicitly covers pair interactions as it extends the array parameter by parameter.

generalfeedback.text: IPOG (In-Parameter-Order Generation) builds a covering array for the first two parameters, then adds one parameter at a time: it horizontally extends existing rows to cover new pairs and vertically adds rows where needed. Like AETG it is a greedy, near-optimal heuristic, not guaranteed minimal.

questiontext.text: What distinguishes an orthogonal array from a general covering array for pairwise testing?

answer.text: An orthogonal array requires each pair to appear the same fixed number of times (balanced); a covering array only requires each pair at least once

feedback.text: Correct — orthogonal arrays are balanced, a stronger special case.

answer.text: An orthogonal array covers three-way combinations while a covering array covers only pairs

feedback.text: The distinction is balance, not strength; both can be defined at strength 2.

answer.text: A covering array must be balanced while an orthogonal array need not be

feedback.text: This reverses the definitions — the orthogonal array is the balanced one.

answer.text: An orthogonal array allows constraints while a covering array forbids them

feedback.text: Constraint handling is unrelated to the balance distinction between the two.

generalfeedback.text: An orthogonal array requires that every pair of values appears exactly the same number of times (λ), making it balanced. A covering array only requires each pair at least once, so it is usually smaller and more flexible. Every orthogonal array is a covering array, but not vice versa.

name.text: Number of pairs for three 3-valued parameters

questiontext.text: Three parameters each have 3 values. How many distinct value-pairs must a pairwise suite cover in total?

feedback.text: Correct — there are 3 parameter-pairs, each contributing 3 × 3 = 9 value-pairs: 3 × 9 = 27.
9 is the value-pairs for a single pair of parameters; there are 3 such parameter-pairs, giving 27.
18 counts only two of the three parameter-pairs; all C(3,2) = 3 pairs of parameters count.
81 would be raising the value count to a power; the total pairs are summed over parameter-pairs: 3 × (3 × 3) = 27.

generalfeedback.text: The number of value-pairs to cover is the sum over each pair of parameters of (v_i × v_j). With 3 parameters there are C(3,2) = 3 parameter-pairs, each contributing 3 × 3 = 9, for 27 in total.

name.text: Number of pairs for 3 x 2 x 2

questiontext.text: Three parameters have domain sizes 3, 2, and 2. How many distinct value-pairs must a pairwise suite cover in total?

feedback.text: 12 is the exhaustive test count (3 × 2 × 2), not the number of value-pairs.
7 is the sum of the domain sizes; the number of pairs sums v_i × v_j over the three parameter-pairs.
10 misses one parameter-pair; the three contributions are 6, 6, and 4, totalling 16.

generalfeedback.text: Sum v_i × v_j over all pairs of parameters: parameters (P1=3, P2=2, P3=2) give P1-P2 = 6, P1-P3 = 6, P2-P3 = 4, for a total of 16 value-pairs.

questiontext.text: Greedy pairwise generators such as AETG and IPOG always produce the smallest possible covering array.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — they are near-optimal heuristics and are not guaranteed to be minimal.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: AETG and IPOG are greedy heuristics; they are fast and near-optimal but not guaranteed to yield the minimum-size array.

generalfeedback.text: Finding a minimum covering array is computationally hard. AETG and IPOG use greedy heuristics that produce small, near-optimal suites quickly, but the result may be larger than the true minimum.

questiontext.text: A system has parameters with domains 3, 3, and 3. Exhaustive testing needs 27 tests. What can we say about a pairwise suite for this system?

answer.text: It needs at least 9 tests (the product of the two largest domains) and typically far fewer than the 27 exhaustive tests

feedback.text: Correct — the lower bound is 3 × 3 = 9, and a good pairwise suite is much smaller than exhaustive.

answer.text: It needs exactly 27 tests, the same as exhaustive

feedback.text: Pairwise is smaller than exhaustive here; 27 is the full product.

answer.text: It needs exactly 3 tests

feedback.text: 3 tests cannot cover all 3 × 3 = 9 pairs of any two of the parameters.

answer.text: It always needs the sum of the domain sizes, 9, exactly

feedback.text: 9 is a lower bound, not always exactly achievable; and it is a product of the two largest domains, not a sum of all.

generalfeedback.text: The pairwise lower bound is the product of the two largest domains: 3 × 3 = 9. A pairwise suite lies between that bound and the exhaustive 27; well-known constructions cover all pairs of three 3-valued parameters in as few as 9 rows, well below exhaustive.

questiontext.text: What is the balance (index λ) property of an orthogonal array of strength 2?

answer.text: Every pair of values from any two columns appears in exactly λ rows

feedback.text: Correct — a fixed λ for every pair is what makes the array balanced.

answer.text: Each column contains every value exactly once

feedback.text: That describes a permutation of a single column, not the two-column balance of an orthogonal array.

answer.text: Every pair of values appears at least once, with no constraint on how often

feedback.text: "At least once" is the covering-array property; orthogonal arrays require exactly λ times.

answer.text: The number of rows equals the number of columns

feedback.text: Rows and columns are independent; balance is about equal pair frequency, not a square shape.

generalfeedback.text: In a strength-2 orthogonal array, for any two columns each ordered pair of values appears in exactly λ rows (λ is the index). This uniform frequency is stronger than the covering-array requirement of "at least once".

name.text: Pairwise lower bound for 4 x 3 x 3 x 2

questiontext.text: A system has four parameters with domain sizes 4, 3, 3, and 2. What is the minimum number of tests any pairwise suite must contain?

answer.text: At least 12

feedback.text: Correct — the two largest domains are 4 and 3, so the bound is 4 × 3 = 12.

answer.text: At least 72

feedback.text: 72 is the exhaustive count (4 × 3 × 3 × 2); pairwise needs far fewer.

answer.text: At least 9

feedback.text: 9 uses 3 × 3; the two largest domains are 4 and 3, giving 12.

answer.text: At least 24

feedback.text: 24 (4 × 3 × 2) uses three domains; the lower bound uses only the two largest, 4 × 3 = 12.

generalfeedback.text: The pairwise lower bound is the product of the two largest domains. Here the largest are 4 and 3, so any pairwise suite needs at least 4 × 3 = 12 rows.

name.text: Orthogonal array is a covering array

questiontext.text: Every orthogonal array of strength 2 is also a valid pairwise covering array.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — if every pair appears exactly λ ≥ 1 times, then in particular every pair appears at least once.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: An orthogonal array covers every pair exactly λ times, so it certainly covers every pair at least once — the covering-array requirement.

generalfeedback.text: An orthogonal array is the balanced special case: each pair appears exactly λ times. Since λ ≥ 1, every pair appears at least once, so the array satisfies pairwise covering. The converse fails: a covering array need not be balanced.

questiontext.text: Why are greedy heuristics like AETG and IPOG used to build pairwise suites instead of computing the exact minimum?

answer.text: Finding a minimum covering array is computationally hard, so greedy methods trade a slightly larger suite for fast, practical generation

feedback.text: Correct — they give near-optimal results quickly where exact minimization is intractable.

answer.text: Greedy methods are the only ones that can guarantee full pairwise coverage

feedback.text: Exact methods also guarantee coverage; greedy methods are chosen for speed, not because they are the only correct option.

answer.text: Greedy methods always find a strictly smaller suite than any exact method

feedback.text: Exact methods find the true minimum; greedy suites are near-optimal and can be larger.

answer.text: Greedy methods avoid covering some pairs, which makes them faster

feedback.text: Both AETG and IPOG still cover all required pairs; they are just heuristic about suite size.

generalfeedback.text: Computing a provably minimum covering array is an NP-hard optimization problem. AETG and IPOG are greedy constructive heuristics that produce small, near-optimal suites in reasonable time while still guaranteeing complete pairwise coverage.

questiontext.text: Both AETG and IPOG are greedy pairwise generators. What is the key difference in how they grow the test suite?

answer.text: AETG adds one complete test row at a time; IPOG adds one parameter (column) at a time, extending and adding rows as needed

feedback.text: Correct — AETG grows row-by-row, IPOG grows parameter-by-parameter.

answer.text: AETG guarantees the minimum suite; IPOG guarantees only pairwise coverage

feedback.text: Neither guarantees minimality; both are near-optimal heuristics that guarantee pairwise coverage.

answer.text: AETG covers only pairs; IPOG covers all combinations exhaustively

feedback.text: Both target pairwise (2-way) coverage; IPOG does not build the exhaustive set.

answer.text: AETG works only for binary parameters; IPOG works for any domain size

feedback.text: Both handle arbitrary domain sizes; the difference is the growth strategy.

generalfeedback.text: AETG constructs the suite one whole row at a time, each row greedily covering as many uncovered pairs as possible. IPOG instead builds an array for the first parameters and then adds one parameter at a time (horizontal growth), adding rows when necessary (vertical growth). Both are greedy and near-optimal, not guaranteed minimal.

questiontext.text: Three boolean flags A, B, C each take values on/off. A fault occurs only when A=on, B=on, and C=on all hold simultaneously. Why can a pairwise suite miss this fault?

answer.text: Pairwise only guarantees each pair (e.g. A=on with B=on) appears, but never guarantees all three on-values occur together in one test

feedback.text: Correct — the triggering triple is a 3-way interaction, which 2-way coverage does not guarantee.

answer.text: Pairwise never tests any flag set to on

feedback.text: Pairwise does test on-values; it just may not put all three on in the same row.

answer.text: Pairwise always tests fewer than three parameters at a time, so C is ignored

feedback.text: All parameters get values in every row; the gap is that the specific triple may never coincide.

answer.text: Pairwise requires each pair to appear exactly once, which excludes the failing combination

feedback.text: Pairwise requires each pair at least once; the issue is 3-way, not a frequency restriction.

generalfeedback.text: A pairwise suite can cover (A=on,B=on), (A=on,C=on), and (B=on,C=on) across different rows without ever placing A=on, B=on, and C=on in the same row. Since the fault needs that exact 3-way combination, pairwise (t = 2) may miss it; detecting it requires t ≥ 3.

name.text: Validity check: does this set cover all pairs (yes)

questiontext.text:
Three binary parameters A, B, C (each 0 or 1). Consider the four rows:
ABC = 000, 011, 101, 110.
Does this set cover every pair of values for every pair of parameters?

answer.text: Yes — all four value-pairs are covered for each of the three parameter-pairs
No — the pair A=1, B=1 is missing

feedback.text: Row 110 has A=1, B=1, so that pair is present.

answer.text: No — the pair B=0, C=0 is missing

feedback.text: Row 000 has B=0, C=0, so that pair is present.

answer.text: No — four rows can never cover all pairs of three binary parameters

feedback.text: Four rows suffice here (the pairwise lower bound is 2 × 2 = 4), and this set achieves it.

generalfeedback.text: Enumerate each parameter-pair. A,B over the rows: (0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1). A,C: (0,0),(0,1),(1,1),(1,0). B,C: (0,0),(1,1),(0,1),(1,0). Each pair-set contains all four combinations, so this is a valid pairwise covering array of just 4 rows — matching the lower bound 2 × 2 = 4.

name.text: Validity check: does this set cover all pairs (no)

questiontext.text:
Three binary parameters A, B, C (each 0 or 1). Consider the three rows:
ABC = 000, 011, 101.
Does this set cover every pair of values for every pair of parameters?

answer.text: No — the pair A=1, B=1 never appears (and other pairs are missing too)

feedback.text: Correct — A,B over the rows gives only (0,0),(0,1),(1,0); (1,1) is missing.

answer.text: Yes — all pairs are covered

feedback.text: The pair A=1,B=1 is absent, so coverage is incomplete.

answer.text: No — but only because A=0, B=0 is missing

feedback.text: Row 000 supplies A=0,B=0; the genuinely missing pair is A=1,B=1.

answer.text: Yes — three rows always suffice for three binary parameters

feedback.text: The pairwise lower bound here is 2 × 2 = 4, so three rows cannot cover all pairs.

generalfeedback.text: A,B over rows 000, 011, 101 gives (0,0),(0,1),(1,0) — the pair (1,1) is never present. (B,C also misses (1,0).) With only three rows you fall below the pairwise lower bound of 2 × 2 = 4, so full pairwise coverage is impossible.

questiontext.text: If a fault is triggered only by a specific combination of three particular parameters, what is the minimum interaction strength t a covering array must have to guarantee detection?

answer.text: t = 3 (three-way coverage)

feedback.text: Correct — a 3-way fault is only guaranteed to be exercised by a strength-3 (or higher) covering array.

answer.text: t = 2 (pairwise) is sufficient

feedback.text: Pairwise guarantees only 2-way combinations; the specific triple may never coincide.

answer.text: t = 1 (each-choice) is sufficient

feedback.text: Each-choice only guarantees each single value appears, far weaker than needed.

answer.text: No covering array can ever guarantee it

feedback.text: A strength-3 covering array guarantees every 3-way combination, including the triggering one.

generalfeedback.text: To guarantee that a specific 3-way value combination is exercised, the covering array must have strength t ≥ 3, since only then is every triple of parameter values guaranteed to appear together in some row.

questiontext.text: A system has ten independent boolean parameters (each on/off). How many tests does exhaustive testing require?

feedback.text: 20 is 2 × 10; exhaustive is 2 raised to the number of parameters, 2^10 = 1024.
100 is 10^2; the base is 2 (values) raised to 10 (parameters): 2^10 = 1024.
4 (2 × 2) is the pairwise lower bound for binary parameters, not the exhaustive count.

generalfeedback.text: Exhaustive is the product of domain sizes: for ten binary parameters that is 2^10 = 1024. A pairwise suite for the same system needs only a handful of rows, illustrating the reduction — while its lower bound stays at just 2 × 2 = 4.

name.text: Pairwise lower bound for 5 x 4 x 3 x 2

questiontext.text: A system has four parameters with domain sizes 5, 4, 3, and 2. What is the minimum number of tests any pairwise suite must contain?

answer.text: At least 20

feedback.text: Correct — the two largest domains are 5 and 4, so the bound is 5 × 4 = 20.

answer.text: At least 120

feedback.text: 120 is the exhaustive count (5 × 4 × 3 × 2); pairwise needs far fewer.

answer.text: At least 15

feedback.text: 15 uses 5 × 3; the two largest domains are 5 and 4, giving 20.

answer.text: At least 60

feedback.text: 60 (5 × 4 × 3) uses three domains; the lower bound uses only the two largest, 5 × 4 = 20.

generalfeedback.text: The pairwise lower bound is the product of the two largest domains: 5 × 4 = 20. (For reference, exhaustive here is 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 = 120.)

name.text: Number of pairs for four binary parameters

questiontext.text: Four parameters are each binary (2 values). How many distinct value-pairs must a pairwise suite cover in total?

feedback.text: Correct — C(4,2) = 6 parameter-pairs, each with 2 × 2 = 4 value-pairs: 6 × 4 = 24.
16 is the exhaustive count (2^4), not the number of value-pairs to cover.
12 would be 3 parameter-pairs × 4; there are C(4,2) = 6 parameter-pairs, giving 24.
8 is 4 parameters × 2 values; the number of value-pairs sums 2 × 2 over all 6 parameter-pairs.

generalfeedback.text: Number of value-pairs = sum over parameter-pairs of v_i × v_j. With four binary parameters there are C(4,2) = 6 parameter-pairs, each contributing 2 × 2 = 4, for 6 × 4 = 24 value-pairs.

questiontext.text: A media player crashes only when the codec is H.265, the container is MKV, and hardware acceleration is enabled — no smaller combination triggers it. A pairwise suite over {codec, container, hw-accel, resolution} was run and passed. What does this tell us?

answer.text: The fault is a genuine 3-way interaction that a 2-way suite is not guaranteed to expose, so passing pairwise does not prove its absence

feedback.text: Correct — the crash needs a specific triple, which pairwise does not guarantee to place in one row.

answer.text: The fault cannot exist, because pairwise testing detects all interaction faults

feedback.text: Pairwise only guarantees 2-way interactions; 3-way faults can slip through.

answer.text: The pairwise suite was invalid, since a correct one would always catch this

feedback.text: A valid pairwise suite covers all pairs but is not required to cover this triple; the suite can be correct yet miss the fault.

answer.text: Only exhaustive testing could ever have run the H.265 codec at all

feedback.text: Pairwise does exercise H.265 in some rows; it just may not combine it with MKV and hw-accel together.

generalfeedback.text: The crash requires the exact triple (H.265, MKV, hw-accel on). A pairwise suite guarantees every pair of these appears, but not necessarily all three in the same test, so it can pass while the 3-way fault remains. Detecting it requires a strength-3 covering array (or exhaustive testing).

name.text: Effect of constraints on valid combinations

questiontext.text: An OS parameter has values {Windows, macOS, Linux} and a browser parameter has {Safari, Chrome, Edge}. A constraint says Safari runs only on macOS, and Edge is excluded on Linux. How do such constraints affect combinatorial test generation?

answer.text: Invalid pairs are removed from the coverage requirement, so the generator must cover only the pairs that satisfy the constraints

feedback.text: Correct — constraints prune infeasible combinations from what must be covered and from generated rows.

answer.text: Constraints are ignored, and every syntactic pair is still forced into the suite

feedback.text: Constraint-aware generation must not emit infeasible rows such as Safari on Linux.

answer.text: Constraints force the suite to become exhaustive

feedback.text: Constraints reduce, not increase, the set of feasible combinations.

answer.text: Constraints require switching from pairwise to each-choice coverage

feedback.text: Pairwise still applies; the generator just excludes infeasible pairs and rows.

generalfeedback.text: Constraints declare certain combinations invalid (e.g. Safari only on macOS). A constraint-aware generator excludes those infeasible pairs from the coverage obligation and never emits a row that violates a constraint, which typically shrinks both the required pairs and the suite.

name.text: Why greedy suites may not be minimal

questiontext.text: Two engineers each run IPOG on the same model but list the parameters in a different order and get pairwise suites of different sizes. What does this illustrate?

answer.text: IPOG is a greedy heuristic whose result depends on choices like parameter order, so it is near-optimal but not guaranteed minimal

feedback.text: Correct — greedy construction can yield different, non-minimal sizes depending on ordering.

answer.text: One of the two suites must be invalid, since a correct suite has a unique size

feedback.text: Both can be valid pairwise suites; valid suites need not all be the same size.

answer.text: Pairwise coverage is undefined when parameter order changes

feedback.text: Pairwise coverage is well-defined regardless of order; only the heuristic's output size varies.

answer.text: The larger suite failed to cover some pairs

feedback.text: Both cover all pairs by construction; the size difference reflects heuristic choices, not missing coverage.

generalfeedback.text: IPOG builds the array incrementally, and decisions such as parameter order affect how efficiently rows get reused. Both suites cover all pairs, but one may be larger — showing the algorithm is near-optimal, not guaranteed to produce the minimum covering array.

questiontext.text: Does a strength-3 (three-way) covering array also satisfy pairwise (2-way) coverage?

answer.text: Yes — if every triple of values is covered, then in particular every pair within those triples is covered

feedback.text: Correct — higher strength subsumes all lower strengths.

answer.text: No — three-way and two-way coverage are unrelated

feedback.text: They are related: covering all triples necessarily covers all pairs.

answer.text: Only if the array is also an orthogonal array

feedback.text: Balance is not required; any strength-3 covering array already covers all pairs.

answer.text: Only if all parameters are binary

feedback.text: The subsumption holds for any domain sizes, not just binary.

generalfeedback.text: A strength-t covering array subsumes all strengths below t: covering every t-tuple guarantees every smaller sub-tuple is covered too. So a 3-way array automatically provides 2-way (pairwise) coverage — at greater cost.

questiontext.text: What does the notation CA(N; 3, k, v) describe?

answer.text: An N-row covering array over k parameters of v values each, in which every 3-way value combination is covered at least once

feedback.text: Correct — the 3 is the strength, so all triples are covered.

answer.text: An array with exactly 3 rows over k parameters

feedback.text: The number of rows is N; the 3 is the interaction strength.

answer.text: An array covering only 3 of the k parameters

feedback.text: All k parameters are covered; strength 3 means every group of 3 has all its combinations covered.

answer.text: An array where each parameter has exactly 3 values

feedback.text: The number of values is v; the 3 in that position is the strength t.

generalfeedback.text: CA(N; 3, k, v) is a covering array with N rows, strength t = 3, k parameters, and v values per parameter, guaranteeing every 3-way combination of values appears in at least one row.

questiontext.text: A fault that is triggered only by a specific three-parameter interaction can pass undetected through an otherwise valid pairwise test suite.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — pairwise guarantees only 2-way combinations, so the triggering triple may never occur in one row.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Pairwise only guarantees 2-way coverage; a fault needing a specific 3-way combination can slip through a valid pairwise suite.

generalfeedback.text: Pairwise (t = 2) guarantees every pair of values appears together, but not every triple. A fault requiring a particular 3-way interaction can therefore escape a fully valid pairwise suite; catching it needs strength t ≥ 3.

questiontext.text: For a system with k parameters, at what interaction strength t does t-way (covering-array) testing become equivalent to exhaustive testing?

answer.text: When t = k (the strength equals the number of parameters)

feedback.text: Correct — covering every k-tuple is exactly the full Cartesian product.

answer.text: When t = 2, since pairwise already covers everything

feedback.text: Pairwise covers pairs, not all full combinations; it is much smaller than exhaustive.

answer.text: When t = 1

feedback.text: t = 1 is each-choice, the weakest criterion, nowhere near exhaustive.

answer.text: t-way testing can never equal exhaustive testing

feedback.text: At t = k every combination of all k parameters must appear, which is exactly exhaustive.

generalfeedback.text: When the strength t equals the number of parameters k, covering every t-tuple means covering every full combination of all parameters — the exhaustive Cartesian product. So exhaustive testing is the t = k case of t-way combinatorial testing.

name.text: Is the lower bound always achievable

questiontext.text: For four binary parameters, the pairwise lower bound is 2 × 2 = 4. Can a pairwise suite of exactly 4 rows actually cover all pairs for four binary parameters?

answer.text: No — 4 rows are impossible here; the true minimum is 5, so the lower bound is not always achievable

feedback.text: Correct — 4 rows can cover all pairs for at most three binary parameters; a fourth forces a fifth row.

answer.text: Yes — the lower bound is always exactly achievable

feedback.text: The product-of-two-largest bound is a lower bound, not always tight; here 4 rows are provably insufficient.

answer.text: No — the true minimum is 16, the exhaustive count

feedback.text: Pairwise needs far fewer than exhaustive; the minimum here is 5, not 16.

answer.text: Yes — but only if the four parameters are statistically independent

feedback.text: Independence does not help; 4 rows cannot cover all six parameter-pairs' combinations for four binary parameters.

generalfeedback.text: Fitting all pairs of four binary parameters into 4 rows would require every pair of columns to show all four combinations exactly once — an orthogonal array of index 1, which for strength 2 admits at most (N-1)/(v-1) = 3 binary factors. A fourth factor cannot fit, so at least 5 rows are needed (and 5 suffices). The lower bound of 4 is therefore not achievable here — it bounds, but does not always equal, the minimum.
